lessons.title: Eukaryotic and prokaryotic cells
lessons.text:
## Eukaryotic and prokaryotic cells
LV: GCSE · Foundation
S: Every living thing is made of cells, and biologists sort cells into two basic designs: eukaryotic cells, which keep their DNA in a nucleus, and prokaryotic cells, which have no nucleus at all. This split underpins the rest of cell biology.
PRE: Cell theory
O: Identify plant and animal cells as eukaryotic and name the parts they share
O: Describe the structure of a bacterial cell, including how its DNA is arranged
O: Compare eukaryotic and prokaryotic cells in structure and size
REQ: aqa-gcse-biology:4.1.1.1.a @1,3
REQ: aqa-gcse-biology:4.1.1.1.b @2,3
T: Eukaryotic cell | A cell whose DNA is enclosed in a nucleus, such as a plant or animal cell
T: Prokaryotic cell | A cell with no nucleus, whose main DNA forms a single loop; bacteria are the GCSE example
T: Plasmid | A small extra ring of DNA, separate from the main DNA loop; a cell may have several
T: Nucleoid | The region of a prokaryotic cell's cytoplasm where its main DNA loop lies, with no membrane around it
H: Two kinds of cell
P: Cells come in two basic types. In a **eukaryotic** cell the DNA is kept inside a **nucleus**. Animals, plants, fungi and protists are all made of eukaryotic cells. A **prokaryotic** cell has no nucleus, and no other structure wrapped in its own membrane. Bacteria are prokaryotes, and so is a second group of single-celled organisms called Archaea.
P: Some parts are found in every cell of either type: a cell membrane around the outside, cytoplasm inside it, DNA, and tiny structures called ribosomes.
H: Plant and animal cells
P: Plant cells and animal cells are both eukaryotic. Each has a **cell membrane** at its edge, **cytoplasm** filling the inside, and a **nucleus** that contains the cell's genetic material. Plant cells also have extra parts, including a cell wall made of cellulose, which animal cells do not have.
D: bio-animal-cell
D: bio-plant-cell
P: The diagrams also show structures such as mitochondria; you will meet those in later lessons. For this topic, focus on the membrane, the cytoplasm and the nucleus.
H: Bacterial cells
P: A bacterium is a prokaryotic cell. Its cytoplasm is enclosed by a cell membrane, and outside the membrane is a **cell wall**. There is no nucleus. Instead, the main DNA forms one **loop** (a closed circle) lying free in the cytoplasm, in a region called the nucleoid. Many bacteria also carry one or more **plasmids**: small, separate rings of DNA that float in the cytoplasm.
- Cell wall: gives the bacterium its shape and protects it. Most bacterial walls are made of peptidoglycan, not cellulose.
- Ribosomes: present, as in all cells.
- Capsule: an extra outer layer that many bacteria have outside the wall (beyond what AQA requires).
- Flagella: structures that some bacteria use for movement (also beyond what AQA requires).
D: bio-prokaryotic-cell
K: Eukaryotic cells (plant and animal) keep their DNA inside a nucleus. Prokaryotic cells (bacteria) have no nucleus: their DNA is one loop in the cytoplasm, often with plasmids, and the cell is surrounded by a membrane with a wall outside it.
H: Comparing the two
- Size: prokaryotic cells are far smaller, roughly 0.1 to 5 micrometres across, while eukaryotic cells are about 10 to 100 micrometres.
- DNA: inside a nucleus in eukaryotic cells; a single loop, plus any plasmids, free in the cytoplasm of prokaryotic cells.
- Membrane-bound structures such as the nucleus: present in eukaryotic cells, absent from prokaryotic cells.
- Cell wall: in plant cells (cellulose) and bacteria (not cellulose), but not in animal cells.
- Shared by both: cell membrane, cytoplasm, DNA and ribosomes.
X: A cell 2 micrometres long has a wall and a loop of DNA in its cytoplasm, but no nucleus. Classify it.
> Look for a nucleus: there is none, so it cannot be a plant or animal cell.
> Check the DNA: a loop lying free in the cytoplasm is the prokaryotic arrangement.
> Check the size: 2 micrometres is inside the 0.1 to 5 micrometre range for prokaryotes and well below the 10 micrometres or more of eukaryotic cells.
> Conclusion: it is a prokaryotic cell, such as a bacterium.
!: Thinking prokaryotes have no DNA. They do have DNA; it simply is not enclosed in a nucleus.
!: Thinking only plant cells have walls. Bacteria have walls too, but theirs are not made of cellulose.
!: Thinking "prokaryote" just means "bacterium". Archaea are prokaryotes as well; bacteria are simply the example used at GCSE.
!: The AQA specification only says that bacteria have a cell wall. Textbooks add that most bacterial walls are made of peptidoglycan. In an AQA exam "cell wall" is enough, but never call it cellulose.
!: Cell sizes are approximate ranges, not fixed values, and sources quote slightly different figures, so give ranges and say "about".
Q: Which part holds the DNA in a plant or animal cell? | The nucleus.
Q: How is the main DNA arranged in a bacterial cell? | As a single loop lying free in the cytoplasm, not inside a nucleus.
Q: What is a plasmid? | A small extra ring of DNA, separate from the main loop, found in many bacteria.
Q: Which four parts do all cells share? | A cell membrane, cytoplasm, DNA and ribosomes.
Q: How does a bacterial cell wall differ from a plant cell wall? | It is not made of cellulose; most bacterial walls are made of peptidoglycan.
Q: Roughly how big are prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells? | Prokaryotic cells are about 0.1 to 5 micrometres across; eukaryotic cells about 10 to 100 micrometres.
M1@1: Which of these cells is eukaryotic? | A cell from a leaf | A bacterium from soil | A bacterium from the gut | An archaean from a hot spring | Plant cells, such as leaf cells, keep their DNA in a nucleus, so they are eukaryotic; bacteria and archaea are prokaryotes.
M1@2: Where is the main DNA found in a bacterial cell? | In a loop free in the cytoplasm | Inside a nucleus in the cytoplasm | Only in plasmids attached to the wall | Nowhere, as bacteria have no DNA | Bacteria have DNA but no nucleus: the main DNA is a single loop in the cytoplasm, and plasmids are extra rings.
M2@2: A student says, "Bacteria have no cell wall, because only plants have walls." Which correction is right? | Bacteria do have walls, but not made of cellulose | Bacteria have walls made of cellulose, like plants | Only animal cells and bacteria lack cell walls | Bacteria have a wall instead of a cell membrane | A bacterial cell has a membrane with a wall outside it; the wall is not made of cellulose, unlike a plant cell wall.
M2@1,3: Which part is found in plant and animal cells but not in bacterial cells? | A nucleus | A cell membrane | Cytoplasm | Ribosomes | All cells have a membrane, cytoplasm and ribosomes; only eukaryotic cells, such as plant and animal cells, have a nucleus.
M3@3: A cell is 50 micrometres across and has a nucleus but no cell wall. Which is it most likely to be? | An animal cell | A plant cell | A bacterial cell | A bacterium with plasmids | A nucleus and a size in the 10 to 100 micrometre range mean the cell is eukaryotic; with no wall it cannot be a plant cell, so it is an animal cell.
M3@2,3: Which statement correctly compares a bacterium with an animal cell? | The bacterium is smaller and its DNA is not in a nucleus | The bacterium is larger and its DNA is in a nucleus | The bacterium is smaller and it has no DNA at all | The bacterium is the same size but lacks a membrane | Bacteria are roughly 0.1 to 5 micrometres, much smaller than animal cells, and their DNA is a loop in the cytoplasm rather than in a nucleus.
SUM: Plant and animal cells are eukaryotic: each has a nucleus holding its DNA, as well as cytoplasm and a cell membrane.
SUM: Bacteria are prokaryotic: they have no nucleus, and their main DNA is one loop in the cytoplasm, often with extra rings called plasmids.
SUM: A bacterial cell has cytoplasm inside a cell membrane, with a cell wall outside the membrane that is not made of cellulose.
SUM: Prokaryotic cells are much smaller than eukaryotic cells, roughly 0.1 to 5 micrometres compared with 10 to 100 micrometres.
SRC: AQA, GCSE Biology 8461 specification (2016), section 4.1.1.1 | standard | 2026-11-25 | https://filestore.aqa.org.uk/resources/biology/specifications/AQA-8461-SP-2016.PDF

lessons.title: Cell size, scale and standard form
lessons.text:
## Cell size, scale and standard form
LV: GCSE · Application
S: Cells are far too small to see with the naked eye, so biologists measure them in micrometres and write their sizes in standard form. Handling these units lets you compare cells and work out how many times bigger one is than another.
PRE: Eukaryotic and prokaryotic cells
PRE: Scientific notation
O: Convert cell sizes between metres, millimetres and micrometres
O: Write very small cell sizes in standard form
O: Compare the sizes of eukaryotic and prokaryotic cells using order of magnitude calculations
REQ: aqa-gcse-biology:4.1.1.1.c @1,2,3
T: Micrometre | One thousandth of a millimetre, or 1 × 10^{-6} m; symbol µm
T: Standard form | A way of writing a number as A × 10^{n}, where A is at least 1 and less than 10
T: Order of magnitude | A factor of ten; two sizes differ by one order of magnitude when one is about 10 times the other
H: Units for tiny things
P: Each step down the scale of length units is a factor of 1000: 1 metre is 1000 millimetres, and 1 millimetre is 1000 micrometres (µm). The prefix *milli* means one thousandth and *micro* means one millionth. Most cells are measured in micrometres: a bacterium is a few micrometres long, while plant and animal cells are tens of micrometres across.
E: 1 m = 1000 mm and 1 mm = 1000 µm :: so a micrometre is one millionth of a metre
- Millimetres to micrometres: multiply by 1000.
- Micrometres to millimetres: divide by 1000.
- Millimetres to metres: divide by 1000.
X: A plant cell is 0.05 mm wide. Give its width in micrometres and in metres.
> Millimetres to micrometres means multiplying by 1000: 0.05 × 1000 = 50, so the cell is 50 µm wide.
> Millimetres to metres means dividing by 1000: 0.05 ÷ 1000 = 0.00005, so the cell is 0.00005 m wide.
H: Standard form
P: A number like 0.000005 m is easy to misread, so very small sizes are written in **standard form**: a number from 1 up to, but not including, 10, multiplied by a power of ten. For a number smaller than 1 the power is negative. Count how many places the decimal point must move to the right to give a number between 1 and 10; that count, with a minus sign, is the power.
X: Write the length of a 2 µm bacterium in metres, in standard form.
> One micrometre is 1 × 10^{-6} m, so 2 µm is 2 × 10^{-6} m.
> Check as a decimal: 0.000002 m. The point moves 6 places to the right to give 2, so the power is −6.
X: An animal cell is 0.00008 m wide. Write this in standard form and in micrometres.
> The point moves 5 places to the right to give 8, so the width is 8 × 10^{-5} m.
> In millimetres: 0.00008 × 1000 = 0.08 mm. In micrometres: 0.08 × 1000 = 80 µm.
K: For cells, think in micrometres: 1 µm is 1 × 10^{-6} m. Always put sizes in the same unit before you compare them.
H: Orders of magnitude
P: An **order of magnitude** is a factor of 10. To compare two sizes, put them in the same unit, divide the larger by the smaller, and see which power of ten the answer is closest to. A ratio of about 10 is one order of magnitude; about 100 is two.
X: How many orders of magnitude wider is a 100 µm plant cell than a 1 µm bacterium?
> Both sizes are already in micrometres.
> Divide: 100 ÷ 1 = 100.
> 100 is 10^{2}, so the plant cell is two orders of magnitude wider.
P: Comparing the two main cell types is a good way to show you understand scale. Prokaryotic cells such as bacteria are about 0.1 to 5 µm across, while eukaryotic cells such as plant and animal cells are about 10 to 100 µm. A typical eukaryotic cell is therefore 10 to 100 times wider, one to two orders of magnitude. To demonstrate this kind of understanding in an exam, set out each calculation step by step: same unit, divide, then name the power of ten.
X: Roughly how many red blood cells, each about 8 µm wide, would fit side by side across a pinhead about 2 mm wide?
> Use one unit: 2 × 1000 = 2000, so the pinhead is about 2000 µm wide.
> Divide: 2000 ÷ 8 = 250.
> So roughly 250 red blood cells would span the pinhead.
DNEED: A scale line stepping down by factors of 10 from 1 mm to 0.1 µm, placing a pinhead (about 2 mm), a plant cell (about 100 µm), a red blood cell (about 8 µm), a bacterium (about 1 to 2 µm) and the light microscope limit (about 200 nm).
H: Why size matters
P: Small cells have a large surface area compared with their volume, so substances can diffuse in and out quickly. As a cell grows, its surface area to volume ratio falls.
P: Scale also limits what we can see. A light microscope shows detail down to about 200 nanometres (nm), an even smaller unit, so the finest structures inside cells need an electron microscope.
!: Mixing units. Convert both sizes to the same unit before dividing: comparing 2 mm with 8 µm directly gives a ratio 1000 times too small.
!: Giving small numbers a positive power. 0.000002 is 2 × 10^{-6}, not 2 × 10^{6}, which would be two million.
!: Treating cell sizes as exact. Real cells vary and sources give slightly different ranges, so use "about" and treat answers as estimates.
Q: How many micrometres are in one millimetre? | 1000.
Q: What is 1 µm in metres, in standard form? | 1 × 10^{-6} m.
Q: What is an order of magnitude? | A factor of 10.
Q: What must you do before dividing one cell size by another? | Convert both sizes to the same unit.
Q: Why can substances move in and out of small cells quickly? | Small cells have a high surface area to volume ratio, so diffusion is fast.
M1@1: How many micrometres wide is a cell that measures 0.02 mm? | 20 µm | 2 µm | 200 µm | 0.00002 µm | To change millimetres into micrometres, multiply by 1000: 0.02 × 1000 = 20.
M2@2: What is 0.000005 m in standard form? | 5 × 10^{-6} m | 5 × 10^{6} m | 5 × 10^{-5} m | 0.5 × 10^{-5} m | The decimal point moves 6 places right to give 5, so the power is −6; 0.5 is not allowed because the first number must be at least 1.
M2@3: A plant cell is 60 µm wide and a bacterium is 0.6 µm long. How many orders of magnitude wider is the plant cell? | 2 | 1 | 3 | 100 | Dividing gives 60 ÷ 0.6 = 100, which is 10^{2}, so two orders of magnitude; 100 is the ratio, not the number of orders.
M3@1,3: About how many 8 µm red blood cells would fit side by side across a line 4 mm long? | 500 | 0.5 | 50 | 5000 | Convert first: 4 × 1000 = 4000, so the line is 4000 µm, and 4000 ÷ 8 = 500. Dividing 4 by 8 without converting gives 0.5.
M3@2,3: A bacterium is 2 × 10^{-6} m long and an animal cell is 2 × 10^{-5} m wide. Which statement is correct? | The animal cell is ten times wider | The bacterium is ten times longer | The animal cell is a hundred times wider | The two cells are the same size | The animal cell is 20 µm and the bacterium 2 µm, so the animal cell is one order of magnitude, ten times, wider.
SUM: One millimetre is 1000 micrometres, and one micrometre is 1 × 10^{-6} m.
SUM: In standard form a small size is written as a number from 1 to just under 10 multiplied by a negative power of ten, such as 2 × 10^{-6} m.
SUM: To compare two cells, put both sizes in the same unit, divide, and express the ratio as a power of ten; a factor of 10 is one order of magnitude.
SUM: A typical eukaryotic cell is one to two orders of magnitude wider than a bacterium.
